title: Research
text:
I investigate properties of complex matter within the framework of statistical and condensed matter physics. I enjoy searching for avenues that translate fundamental principles into modern technological applications. Broadly, my present research interests are in quantum sensing with cavity quantum materials [can we mine the quantum resources within quantum materials by coupling them to quantum light?], machine learning [a grand manifestation of classical (and sometimes quantum) complex systems], quantum criticality [foundational organizing principle; generates some of the most unusual behaviors of matter], and topological materials [a frontier for correlation physics and non-equilibrium phenomena].
My work can be divided into 3 phases based on its primary focus.
The broad topics that I have worked on are summarized by the TOC on the right with publications details below.

title: Shouvik Sur
text:
I am a theoretical physicist with expertise in computational many-body physics. I am interested in the mechanisms and diagnostics of emergent behaviors of complex matter.
My past research has focused on quantum states that arise from the competition between mutually frustrating interactions, and, consequently, often defy conventional frameworks for classifying quantum matter.
I am currently working on many-body aspects of quantum technologies and machine learning. Along the first direction, I am (i) developing new kinds of quantum sensors on cavity quantum materials platforms that can harness the high quantum resources intrinsic to quantum materials [builds on Nature Commun. 17, 4404 (2026)]; (ii) exploring the efficiency of polymorphic quantum hardware for optimizing over independent tasks [builds on arXiv:2604.21913 (2026)]. Along the second direction, (i) I study ML algorithms and architectures using the methods of statistical physics and dynamical systems to develop a controlled understanding of training dynamics and memory; (ii) I develop computational methods, based on machine learning algorithms, to access new regimes of strongly correlated systems and quantum transport in numerical experiments.

title: Neural network representation of Boolean circuits
text:
Most standard 2-bit gates can be represented by a single layer perceptron (SLP). These include the AND, OR, NAND, and NOR gates. This can be understood geometrically by considering the 2-bit dataset \(\mathcal S  = \{0,1\}^2\) as coordinates of the corners of a square. These four gates classify \(\mathcal S\) by “drawing” one decision boundary.
By contrast, the classification performed by XOR will require two decision boundaries. Consequently, XOR cannot be represented by an SLP and the minimal neural network requires one hidden layer with two neurons. This results in a depth 2 neural circuit for representing and learning XOR.
Interestingly, since NAND is a universal gate, it is possible to represent XOR by a circuit of four NAND gates. This circuit of logical gates, however, has depth 3. Here, we show how to negotiate this mismatch of circuit depth, and in the process develop insights into compressing logical-gate circuits to match the minimal MLP implementations of the same function. We anticipate such compressions are maximal for tasks that are “hard” for logical gates but “easy” for MLPs due to the inherent non-linearity of the latter.


A linear threshold function (LTF) performs a linear transformation on its inputs and outputs a binary result based on a threshold condition. AND, OR, NAND, and NOR gates are examples of LTFs. In order to verify the statement, let us obtain the functional representation of these gates. We will consider a function \(f(\vec x) = \Theta(\vec w \cdot \vec x + b)\) with \(\vec w\) and \(b\) being parameters, \(\Theta\) the Heaviside step function, and the two dimensional vector \(\vec x \in \mathcal S\). Note that \(f(\vec x)\) is an SLP with a single neuron and two inputs, characterized by the weights \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), and the bias \(b\). By utilizing the truth table of the respective gates, we can place restrictions on \(\vec w\) and \(b\) as follows.

constrains the parameters of the SLP/LTF as follows

\(f((0, 0)) < 0 \Rightarrow b < 0\),
\(f((0, 1)) > 0 \Rightarrow w_2 > -b\),
\(f((1, 0)) > 0 \Rightarrow w_1 > -b\),
\(f((1, 1)) < 0 \Rightarrow w_1 + w_2 < -b\).

These conditions are mutually incompatible, which implies \(f(\vec x)\) cannot represent XOR. This necessitates the introduction of a hidden layer in the neural network, promoting the SLP to an MLP.


The weights of the hidden layer with two neurons is encoded by the \(2\times 2\) matrix \(\hat W^{(1)}\), and the bias by \(\vec b^{(1)}\), such that the logit is given by \(\vec z^{(1)} = \hat W^{(1)} \vec x + \vec b^{(1)}\). The output layer operates on \(x^{(1)}_i = \Theta(z^{(1)}_i)\) and produces the logit \(z^{(2)} = \hat W^{(2)} \vec x^{(1)} +  b^{(2)}\), where \(\hat W^{(2)}\) is a \(1 \times 2\) matrix (i.e. a row vector). Therefore, the final output is
\[
f(\vec x) = \Theta\left(\sum_{i=1,2} W^{(2)}_i \Theta\left(W^{(1)}_{i1} x_1 + W^{(1)}_{i2} x_2 + b^{(1)}_n \right) +  b^{(2)}  \right)
\tag{1}\]
A solution for the parameters of the MLP that allows \(f(\vec x)\) to represent XOR is
\[
\hat W^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 2 \\
1/2 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
\vec b^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 \\
-3/4
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
\hat W^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix}
3/2 & -1
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
b^{(2)} = -  1
\tag{2}\] which leads to \[
f(\vec x) = \Theta\left(\frac{3}{2} \Theta\left(2 (x_1 + x_2) -1 \right) - \Theta\left((x_1 + x_2)/2  - 3/4 \right) - 1  \right)
\]
In PyTorch this MLP is given by
class XORModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.main=nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(2, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.main(x)



Four NAND gates represent XOR as \[
x_1 \oplus x_2 = \overline{y_1 \land y_2}
\tag{3}\] where \(y_n = \overline{\overline{x_1 \land x_2} \land x_n}\). The maximum order of nesting of the Boolean operations in the expression of \(x_1 \oplus x_2\) corresponds to the number of layers. Naively, since each NAND gate correspond to an LTF and each LTF corresponds to a layer of an MLP, it would appear that one needs a three-layered MLP to represent XOR.
The redundancy is eliminated by noticing that \(y_n\) is, in fact, representable by a single LTF, not a nested LTF. To see this, we simplify \(y_n\) as
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_n &= \overline{\overline{x_1 \land x_2} \land x_n} \\
&= \overline{(\bar{x}_1 \land x_n) \land (\bar{x}_2 \land x_n)} \\
&= \overline{(\bar{x}_2 \land x_1)} ~\delta_{n,1} + \overline{(\bar{x}_1 \land x_2)} ~\delta_{n,2} \\
&= ({x}_2 \lor \bar{x}_1) ~\delta_{n,1} + ({x}_1 \lor \bar{x}_2) ~\delta_{n,2} \\
&= f({x}_2 - {x}_1 + 1/2) ~\delta_{n,1} + f({x}_1 - {x}_2 + 1/2) ~\delta_{n,2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\] Therefore, applying the reduction in Equation 4 to Equation 3 we find that XOR indeed requires a single nesting of LTFs and the circuit depth matches that obtained with the MLP representation of XOR.

The output layer operates on \(x^{(1)}_i = \Theta(z^{(1)}_i)\) and produces the logit \(z^{(2)} = \hat W^{(2)} \vec x^{(1)} +  b^{(2)}\), where \(\hat W^{(2)}\) is a \(1 \times 2\) matrix (i.e. a row vector). Therefore, the final output is
\[
f(\vec x) = \Theta\left(\sum_{i=1,2} W^{(2)}_i \Theta\left(W^{(1)}_{i1} x_1 + W^{(1)}_{i2} x_2 + b^{(1)}_n \right) +  b^{(2)}  \right)
\tag{1}\]
A solution for the parameters of the MLP that allows \(f(\vec x)\) to represent XOR is
\[
\hat W^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & 2 \\
1/2 & 1/2
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
\vec b^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix}
-1 \\
-3/4
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
\hat W^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix}
3/2 & -1
\end{bmatrix}; \qquad
b^{(2)} = -  1
\tag{2}\] which leads to \[
f(\vec x) = \Theta\left(\frac{3}{2} \Theta\left(2 (x_1 + x_2) -1 \right) - \Theta\left((x_1 + x_2)/2  - 3/4 \right) - 1  \right)
\]
In PyTorch this MLP is given by
class XORModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.main=nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(2, 1),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.main(x)



Four NAND gates represent XOR as \[
x_1 \oplus x_2 = \overline{y_1 \land y_2}
\tag{3}\] where \(y_n = \overline{\overline{x_1 \land x_2} \land x_n}\). The maximum order of nesting of the Boolean operations in the expression of \(x_1 \oplus x_2\) corresponds to the number of layers. Naively, since each NAND gate correspond to an LTF and each LTF corresponds to a layer of an MLP, it would appear that one needs a three-layered MLP to represent XOR.
The redundancy is eliminated by noticing that \(y_n\) is, in fact, representable by a single LTF, not a nested LTF. To see this, we simplify \(y_n\) as
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_n &= \overline{\overline{x_1 \land x_2} \land x_n} \\
&= \overline{(\bar{x}_1 \land x_n) \land (\bar{x}_2 \land x_n)} \\
&= \overline{(\bar{x}_2 \land x_1)} ~\delta_{n,1} + \overline{(\bar{x}_1 \land x_2)} ~\delta_{n,2} \\
&= ({x}_2 \lor \bar{x}_1) ~\delta_{n,1} + ({x}_1 \lor \bar{x}_2) ~\delta_{n,2} \\
&= f({x}_2 - {x}_1 + 1/2) ~\delta_{n,1} + f({x}_1 - {x}_2 + 1/2) ~\delta_{n,2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\] Therefore, applying the reduction in Equation 4 to Equation 3 we find that XOR indeed requires a single nesting of LTFs and the circuit depth matches that obtained with the MLP representation of XOR.
